content: 1. The Tier 4 international goals include an annual average interim target (IT-1) of 35 µg/m³ for particulate matter and a 24-hour average of 7 mg/m³ for carbon monoxide. These targets were determined using an earlier version of the single-zone model described in Review 3. 2. The second goal of the International Workshop Agreement (IWA) is to provide flexibility for organizations and countries to select indicators and tiers based on their local priorities, enabling the framework to be applied globally. 3. The third goal is to establish a structure that harmonizes different test protocols used across various countries. Efforts to create performance tiers for other protocols are ongoing. 4. Several countries and organizations have already started using the IWA as a foundation for developing national and organizational standards. 5. To update the initial IWA guidelines and establish them as international standards, the sector has been working through ISO processes. ISO Technical Committee (TC) 285, which is responsible for developing and approving these standards, was established in June 2013. 6. Kenya, through the Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS), and the United States, through the American National Standards Institute (ANSI), serve as co-secretariats of the committee. 7. As of July 2014, the committee included 20 participating countries, 14 observing countries, and 7 international external liaison organizations, including the World Health Organization (WHO). 8. Standards-related activities and drafting of standards are conducted by working groups of experts within the committee, with drafts presented for approval through ISO TC 285. 9. Testing is a critical component of technology development, as it facilitates communication of stove performance to implementers, donors, government programs, and users. It also allows for the evaluation of technologies against standards, including their potential to meet indoor air quality guidelines. 10. Third-party testing is particularly important to ensure unbiased results. Testing can be conducted in controlled laboratory environments or under realistic conditions in homes, where parameters may be harder to control. 11. Both laboratory and field testing are necessary to evaluate whether technologies under consideration can achieve indoor air quality guidelines, as results from these two settings do not always correlate well. 12. Achieving indoor air quality guidelines depends on both technology performance and user behavior, making it essential to evaluate both factors. 13. More laboratory and field testing capacity is needed, especially in developing countries where the use of solid fuels for cooking and the resulting household air pollution (HAP) are significant concerns. 14. Efforts are underway to establish regional testing and knowledge centers (RTKCs) through grants and training workshops. These centers aim to provide high-quality testing services and catalyze regional activities. 15. These centers are collaborating as a consortium to standardize methods, establish best practices, and create common data formats for sharing testing results. 16. Challenges remain in data management and quality assurance testing to ensure more standardized results. 17. Significant progress has been made in protocol development and standardization, particularly through the ongoing ISO TC 285 international standards process. 18. Protocols are being developed to evaluate the robustness of technologies under various usage conditions and to improve protocols to better reflect actual use in homes. 19. Carbon finance has driven significant activity in the clean cooking sector, with methodologies for evaluating technologies often overlapping with those used for assessing carbon impacts. 20. Emerging opportunities exist to include health impacts in climate-based investments, which could further incentivize clean cooking initiatives. 21. The new phase of standards development should focus on harmonizing methodologies, whether for carbon impact assessment, national testing and certification for health improvement, or other purposes. 22. Capacity building for testing and protocol development should be complemented by systems and resources to share test data with the sector, consumers, investors, donors, and programs. 23. There is widespread agreement on the need for comprehensive and transparent resources that indicate how current technologies and fuels perform in both laboratory and field settings. 24. An online global database provides information on stove and fuel features, specifications, emissions levels, efficiency, and safety derived from laboratory and field testing. This platform allows manufacturers to share product information and testing organizations to share independent performance data. 25. The database can be easily updated with new data submitted by manufacturers and testing organizations. 26. Mechanisms for regulation and certification are essential to implement and enforce standards and communicate technology quality and performance to users. 27. Adoption of standards reflecting these guidelines can regulate technologies that are imported or manufactured locally. The tiered indicators in the standards framework allow for stricter standards over time as more advanced technologies become available. 28. Certification processes are necessary to ensure credible and standardized reporting and labeling. National organizations with the mandate and expertise to carry out product certification should be engaged to implement standards and certify technologies for their potential to meet indoor air quality targets. 29. Certification can apply to products to evaluate performance and quality, as well as to testing centers to assess their ability to produce reliable results. 30. Labels serve as a means of communicating technology performance and quality to users. The effectiveness of labels depends on how well the information is presented, whether consumer awareness campaigns are associated, and whether the labeling system is enforced to minimize counterfeiting. 31. Studies are needed to evaluate appropriate label designs and their impact on consumer decisions. 32. The WHO air quality guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations to reduce the health burden associated with household fuel combustion. These guidelines also aim to secure additional societal, developmental, and environmental benefits, including climate benefits from wider access to clean, safe, and efficient household energy. 33. The guidelines are targeted at public health policymakers and specialists working across energy, environment, and other sectors to develop and implement policies that reduce the adverse health impacts of household fuel combustion. 34. This publication is linked to ongoing WHO efforts to provide technical support for implementing the recommendations, monitoring progress, and evaluating program impacts.
